I ran out of tool calls before I could read every source. These notes cover only what I found, and some verses have little or nothing. I couldn't read the full Enduring Word page; I worked from the long extract the search returned. I found nothing at all on vv. 10–11 and 20.

## 1–2. What the traditional commentators say, verse by verse

**Background to vv. 1–12.** Guzik (Enduring Word) says Paul is defending himself because he had many enemies in Thessalonica (Acts 17:5-6 and 17:13) who discredited him in his absence, especially because of his hurried departure. Drawing on Barclay, he lists the charges each verse answers: Paul was deluded (v. 3), had impure motives (v. 3), deceived people (v. 3), pleased people rather than God (v. 4), was in it for money (vv. 5, 9), wanted glory (v. 6) and acted like a dictator (v. 7). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- A different view: The Gospel Coalition's review of Shogren's commentary says Shogren reads 1 Thessalonians 2:1–12 is not apologetic but rather a presentation of the apostles' character that the Thessalonians should imitate. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/1-and-2-thessalonians/

**v. 1:** Guzik reads "not in vain" as being about what kind of ministry it was, not whether it worked: Paul's visit was not empty or hollow, as if he were a mere salesman or marketer. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Chrysostom takes "not vain" to mean the visit was not merely human or ordinary. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm
- A bible.org study says the Greek word *kenos* can mean empty and without truth, or without result. https://bible.org/series/ense?page=1668

**v. 2:** Guzik notes that Paul arrived with his back still wounded from Philippi. Paul would not have kept going through beatings if he were in it for himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Chrysostom makes the same point: nobody would choose such suffering for earthly gain. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm

**v. 3:** Guzik says Paul made the gospel attractive but never changed its core: human need, the Saviour, the cross, the resurrection. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Matthew Henry says Paul's message was pure in content and honest in delivery. He did not say one thing while intending another. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Chrysostom contrasts Paul with the tricks of jugglers and sorcerers and with rebels like Theudas. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm

**v. 4:** Henry treats ministers as stewards who will have to give an account, and says God cannot be pleased where sincerity is missing. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Chrysostom argues that God would not have trusted them with the gospel if He had seen worldly motives in them. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm

**v. 5:** Chrysostom notices a detail. On flattery, which people could see, Paul calls the readers as witnesses ("as you know"). On greed, which was hidden, he calls God as witness. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm
- Henry says the apostles did not win people's affection for themselves by flattering or fawning. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm

**v. 6:** Guzik says Paul did not need praise because his security and acceptance came from Jesus. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Chrysostom says that, as ambassadors from heaven, the apostles could rightly have claimed honour. They simply chose not to. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm

**v. 7:** Guzik says the nursing-mother picture shows Paul's authority was about tender care, not power or control. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Chrysostom says "among you" means "as one of you," and that a teacher should be like a nurse, who neither flatters for glory nor asks her children for money. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_thessalonians/2.htm
- Bible Hub connects the image to Isaiah 66:13. https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/2.htm
- **Textual question ("gentle" or "little children"):**
  - The NET Bible notes say "little children" has much stronger manuscript support. It is also the harder reading, so scribes probably softened it to "gentle." https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php?book=1th&chapter=2&verse=7
  - Jamieson, Fausset & Brown preferred "gentle," because Paul would hardly call himself both an infant and a nursing mother in one sentence. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
  - Shogren, per the TGC review, also reads "little children." https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/review/1-and-2-thessalonians/

**v. 8:** Chrysostom says giving their own souls was harder than preaching the gospel. Paul would have spent his life for them if he could. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/230402.htm
- Guzik says these sacrifices were not a burden to Paul. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/

**v. 9:** Guzik says Paul had a right to be paid (1 Cor 9:14) but gave it up, to set himself apart from teachers of false religions. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Henry says "night and day" doesn't mean nonstop manual work. Paul gave up part of his night's rest so he could minister in the daytime. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Chrysostom compares it to Jacob toiling night and day over his flocks. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_thessalonians/2.htm

**v. 12:** Henry says to "exhort" means to stir people to do their duty, and to "comfort" means to cheer them through difficulties. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Bible Hub explains *parakaleō* as "call alongside" and connects the father image to Deuteronomy 1:31. https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/2.htm
- Guzik says Paul could point to his own life as an example of Jesus' power at work. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/

**v. 13:** Henry says the word comes through weak human messengers but really is God's word. He also says people who pass off their own ideas as God's word are badly at fault. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Precept Austin says the phrase means a spoken message, and that for about 30 years apostolic teaching spread mainly through preaching. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1thessalonians_213
- Ellicott (on Bible Hub) says the word has no effect unless the hearer believes. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_thessalonians/2-13.htm
- Guzik says the Thessalonians were willing to suffer because they were sure it was God's word, not man's. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/

**v. 14:** Gill says the "countrymen" were the rougher sort of Thessalonians, stirred up by unbelieving Jews (Acts 17). https://studylight.org/bible/eng/ncv/1-thessalonians/2-14.html
- Constable thinks "the Jews" probably means the unbelievers who opposed the Christians, not Jews in general. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/2-14.html
- Henry says the Jews of Judea were the first to hear the gospel and the first to persecute it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm

**v. 15:** Bible Hub's Q&A says this is not a blanket condemnation of the Jewish people. It points to particular hostile groups, noting that Paul was Jewish himself and loved his people (Rom 9:1–3). https://biblehub.com/q/why_does_1_thess._2_14-15_blame_jews.htm
- Barclay notes that in the ancient world Jews were accused of "hatred of the human race." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-thessalonians/2-16.html

**v. 16:** Guzik says the opponents were angry that Gentiles could be saved without first becoming Jews. "Wrath" is meant to comfort believers that God will deal with persecutors, so they should not pay back persecution in kind. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/
- Henry says nothing fills up a people's sins faster than blocking the gospel. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Th/1Th_002.cfm
- Bible Hub connects "fill up their sins" to Genesis 15:16, where the Amorites' sin had to reach its full measure. https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/2.htm

**v. 17:** Chrysostom notes that the Greek word means "made orphans." Paul longs for them like children who have lost their parents, and he keeps them always in mind. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_thessalonians/2.htm

**v. 18:** Guzik says Paul could mention Satan without explaining, which shows he had already taught these new converts about spiritual warfare. He also says Satan's roadblock produced Paul's letters, which turned out to be a greater blessing than a visit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-thessalonians-2/

**v. 19:** Chrysostom says "crown" alone was not strong enough, so Paul added "of boasting." Paul rejoices in the church he planted more than in any crown. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/chrysostom/1_thessalonians/2.htm
- Bible Hub: people are the crown, so relationships can have lasting value (Phil 4:1). https://biblehub.com/1_thessalonians/2.htm

## Where Protestant traditions differ

I didn't find any denominational disagreement within Protestantism on this chapter. I found nothing from Lutheran, Methodist or Wesleyan, or Anglican sites. The sources I did read (Guzik, who is on the Pentecostal/charismatic list; Henry; Constable, a dispensationalist; Hiebert) all read the chapter in much the same way.

## Other views

**vv. 13–16, modern scholarship (were these verses added later?):**
- bible.org lists scholars such as Baur, Pearson and Koester who argue that vv. 13–16 were inserted later. Their reasons include the claim that Paul never blames Jews for Jesus' death elsewhere. https://bible.org/article/1-thessalonians-213-16-interpolation
- The author replies that no manuscript, early translation or Church Father leaves the verses out, so the theory should be a last resort. He also argues the section explains why Paul was so anxious to visit again (vv. 17–20). https://bible.org/article/1-thessalonians-213-16-interpolation
- Another bible.org introduction says that even if it were granted, this would not overturn Paul's authorship of the letter. https://bible.org/book/export/html/1335

**v. 13, Catholic reading:**
- Catholic Answers lists this verse among passages that put apostolic teaching handed down by word of mouth on the same level as written Scripture. https://www.catholic.com/magazine/print-edition/oral-tradition-in-the-new-testament
- In a Catholic Answers debate, Trent Horn argues the verse contradicts the idea that God's word comes only in written form. https://www.catholic.com/audio/cot/is-the-catholic-church-a-masterpiece-of-deception

**Orthodox, and prosperity, word of faith or hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on either.
